newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FORECAST - Telebras net seen surging in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Telebras net seen surging in 1997.

text.p: Rate hikes, line growth and greater phone use will boost consolidated earnings for Brazil's telecoms giant Telebras by $1 billion next year to at least $3.78 billion, analysts said.
"Profits will continue to rise sharply, mostly as a result of the tariff increase," said Guilherme Oliveira, an analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Brazil unit.
A Reuters survey of local and foreign analysts showed estimates for Telebras' 1997 consolidated net ranged from $3.783 billion to $4.0 billion.
The projections are up sharply from forecasts for the firm's 1996 earnings of between $2.746 billion and $2.92 billion. Figures for both years are inflation-adjusted.
Telecomunicacoes Brasileiras S.A., the largest publicly traded company in Latin America, is slated to be broken up and sold off in coming years under Brazil's sweeping privatization program.
With 27 local operators and overseas and interstate long-distance monopoly Embratel, Telebras has a market capitalization of about $23 billion and controls 90 percent of Brazil's total phone lines.
The firm is expected to be divided into four or five "Baby Brases" ahead of privatization, expected to begin as early as 1998.
Last month, Telebras reported consolidated earnings of 1.803 billion reais ($1.765 billion) for the January-August period versus 809 million reais net consolidated income in all of 1995.

The sharp increase was due mostly to a steady, strong flow of revenues since last December's hike in residential and commercial rates, as well as increases in traffic and fixed and cellular lines, officials said.
The company is expected to release third-quarter figures before mid-November, with analysts' estimates for the period ranging from $689 million to $730 million.
Few surprises are expected between now and the end of the year, and analysts say any tariff adjustment late this year will not significantly affect 1996 results.

Rather, hikes in local fixed line and cellular rates sometime between November and January are expected to fuel sky-rocketing profits next year, with differences in earnings forecasts stemming mainly from differences in how analysts are calculating the impact of tariff increases.

Analysts project the government will raise the basic residential subscription rate at least 50 percent, the basic non-residential subscription 25-50 percent and the local cellular rate by about 10 percent.
Domestic long-distance rates were seen stable, while international rates were seen stable to dropping in the tariff adjustment, they added.
The company's profits also will swell due to the addition of up to 1.5 million, or nearly 12 percent more in-service fixed lines and one million in-service cellular lines, analysts said.
They also cited across-the-board increases in telecom traffic, particularly in long-distance and cellular calls.
Analysts said the privatization late this year of Brazil's B Band cellular frequency is unlikely to affect 1997 results because new concessionaires will not begin operating until late in 1997.
